At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3368)
response:
Embedding space anisotropy refers to the phenomenon where token representations in a trained LLM cluster into a narrow cone of the high-dimensional space rather than distributing isotropically — and the central diagnostic question is whether this geometric collapse is a signature of memorization (the model has compressed training examples into tight attractor basins) or an artifact of generalization (the model has learned a low-dimensional manifold that genuinely captures linguistic structure). The key concepts are: the average cosine similarity between random embedding pairs (which approaches 1.0 under severe anisotropy rather than ~0 as geometry would predict), the intrinsic dimensionality of the representation manifold, and the distinction between token-level anisotropy (static embeddings) and contextual anisotropy (the distribution of hidden states across a corpus). The expert worry that a beginner entirely misses is that anisotropy is not monolithic — a model can exhibit strong global anisotropy (all representations pulled toward a dominant subspace) while maintaining local isotropy within semantic neighborhoods, meaning coarse cosine-similarity diagnostics will badly mislead you about whether specific examples are memorized. A further subtlety is that anisotropy can be induced by training objective rather than data exposure: next-token prediction loss creates a frequency-weighted pressure that pushes high-frequency token representations toward the origin and collapses the effective rank of the embedding matrix independently of any memorization dynamic. Distinguishing these causal pathways — objective-induced collapse versus memorization-induced collapse versus genuine low-dimensional structure — requires probing the curvature of the representation manifold, not just its global spread statistics.

The cleanest intervention is a controlled duplication experiment: take a fixed corpus, create a version with a subset of documents repeated k times (k = 10, 100, 1000), train otherwise-identical models on the original versus the duplicated corpus, and measure the change in local intrinsic dimensionality (using TwoNN or MLE estimators) specifically within the neighborhood of representations corresponding to duplicated sequences — Kandpal et al. (2022) used exactly this duplication structure to study memorization rates, and the geometric analog is underexplored but tractable. The objective-induced component is held constant across both runs (same architecture, same loss, same token frequency marginals if you're careful), so any differential anisotropy localized to duplicated-sequence representations is causally attributable to memorization pressure rather than loss geometry. A second orthogonal intervention is learning rate rewinding with selective replay: train to convergence, then continue training only on the candidate memorized subset at a low learning rate — the resulting drift in representation geometry (measured as the principal angle between the pre- and post-replay embedding subspaces) isolates the memorization footprint without altering the global frequency statistics that drive objective-induced collapse. Henighan et al.'s scaling work implicitly shows that representation rank scales predictably with compute budget under normal training; deviations from that scaling law in the duplicated-document neighborhood are thus a clean residual signal. The hardest confound to eliminate is frequency co-variation: duplicating documents raises the unigram frequency of their constituent tokens, which itself drives anisotropy through the softmax bottleneck, so the intervention requires either subword-level frequency matching or working in the contextual (hidden-state) embedding space where token identity is partially abstracted away.

Spatial localization is lethal to whole-space metrics as memorization detectors for a simple volumetric reason: if memorized content constitutes even 5–10% of training tokens (a realistic figure for the duplicated-document regimes studied by Carlini et al. 2023), the geometric signal from those subregions is swamped by the billions of non-memorized representations when you compute a global average cosine similarity or fit a covariance matrix to the full embedding cloud — the metric will faithfully track objective-induced anisotropy and be nearly blind to the memorization component. Spectral decay diagnostics have an additional failure mode: the dominant eigenvectors of the embedding covariance are determined by the highest-variance directions, which correspond to the most frequent semantic axes (topic, syntax, register), not to the low-volume high-density clusters where memorized sequences concentrate; a memorization-induced subspace may contribute only to eigenvectors 50–200, well below the threshold where anyone looks. Ethayarajh (2019) showed that BERT, GPT-2, and ELMo all exhibit strong global anisotropy (average cosine similarity 0.6–1.0 depending on layer), but this finding is derived from uniformly sampled token representations — it structurally cannot distinguish a model that memorizes 1% of its corpus from one that memorizes 0%, because the sampling dilutes the memorized subregion into invisibility. What would work is a stratified local metric: partition the embedding space using a high-resolution clustering (e.g., k-means with k ~ 10,000), compute intrinsic dimensionality or cosine concentration within each cluster, and flag clusters whose local anisotropy significantly exceeds the global baseline — this recovers the localized signal that whole-space methods wash out. The implication is that whole-space spectral metrics are better understood as diagnostics of training regime (objective, architecture, data mixture) rather than memorization per se, and repurposing them as memorization detectors without localization is a category error that produces both high false-negative rates on localized memorization and uninterpretable false positives driven by frequency effects.

A concrete operational test is to fit a linear probe for a structured property within the candidate cluster: for number tokens you can recover ordinal rank with R² > 0.95 using a single linear direction (as Geva et al. 2020 and subsequent arithmetic probing work confirms), but a memorization cluster formed by repeated verbatim passages will have no analogous recoverable latent structure — the probe accuracy for any non-trivial semantic relation will be near chance. A second geometric discriminator is the local fractal dimension profile: semantic clusters exhibit smooth intrinsic dimensionality as you expand the neighborhood radius (the TwoNN estimate stabilizes), while memorization attractors show a characteristic dimensionality collapse at small radii followed by a jump as the neighborhood expands past the memorized basin into surrounding generalization territory — this discontinuity in the d(r) curve is a fingerprint of a non-natural cluster. A third signal is generation-conditioned density: if you prompt the model with prefixes drawn from inside the cluster and measure output entropy, memorization clusters will show entropy collapse (the model locks onto a specific continuation) while semantic clusters will show diverse, high-entropy completions consistent with the concept — Carlini et al.'s extraction experiments implicitly exploit exactly this entropy collapse, and you can invert it as a cluster-classification criterion. Together these three tests — structured probe accuracy, fractal dimension discontinuity, and generation entropy — form a diagnostic battery that is robust to the confound because they exploit the cause of the density (structure versus repetition) rather than the density itself.

The practical reformulation involves three steps: first, encode the candidate example and retrieve its k-nearest neighbors in the contextual embedding space (at a middle layer, e.g., layer 16–24 of a 32-layer model where memorization signals are strongest per Hernandez et al. 2023); second, compute the TwoNN intrinsic dimensionality estimate within that neighborhood and compare it against the layer-specific baseline distribution established on held-out non-training data; third, run greedy decoding from the example's prefix and measure the mean per-token entropy of the first 50 generated tokens, flagging entropy below a threshold calibrated on known non-members. This geometric MIA has a structural advantage over loss-threshold tests because it is reference-model-free — Carlini's likelihood ratio attack requires a second model trained on the same distribution, which is expensive and often unavailable, whereas the local geometry query needs only the target model and a neighborhood oracle. The approach connects directly to the Feldman (2020) long-tail memorization theory: examples that require memorization (rare or unique training instances) are precisely those that will form isolated low-dimensionality attractors rather than blending into high-dimensional semantic manifolds, predicting that geometric MIA should show the largest advantage over loss-threshold methods exactly on the long-tail examples where loss-based methods fail most severely. The main practical complication is layer selection sensitivity: the memorization attractor signal is not uniform across depth, and choosing the wrong layer can make the geometric test worse than the loss threshold, so the reformulation requires either a learned layer-weighting scheme or a multi-layer aggregation that pools the intrinsic dimensionality signal across layers 12–28 to reduce sensitivity to this hyperparameter.

A model trained on a flatter data distribution becomes geometrically harder to audit for memorization, and the mechanism is precise: the attractor basin contrast that makes long-tail memorization detectable depends on the difference in local density between the memorized example's neighborhood and the surrounding manifold — when the training distribution is uniform, that surrounding manifold is itself denser and more isotropic, compressing the contrast ratio that the TwoNN estimator exploits, so the intrinsic dimensionality signal shrinks toward the noise floor. Feldman and Zhang (2020) quantified that memorization of individual examples scales with their rarity in the training distribution — examples appearing once in 10M tokens require near-verbatim memorization for accurate prediction, while examples appearing 100+ times do not — which means a uniform distribution, by construction, pushes more examples into the high-frequency regime where generalization suffices and memorization attractors never form, reducing the geometric audit target to a smaller and subtler residual. The counterintuitive implication is that data deduplication, which is usually framed as a privacy protection measure, may paradoxically make the remaining memorization harder to detect geometrically by flattening the distribution and eliminating the long-tail examples whose attractor basins were the strongest audit signal — Lee et al.'s deduplication of C4 and The Pile reduced extractable memorization by ~10x but also eliminated most of the high-contrast geometric targets. A model trained on web text (highly skewed, Zipfian) like GPT-2 or LLaMA's pretraining corpus thus presents a more geometrically auditable vulnerability profile than a hypothetical model trained on a carefully balanced dataset, not because it memorizes more in aggregate, but because its memorization is concentrated in high-contrast attractor basins that stand out against a sparse long-tail background. The practical implication for auditors is that vulnerability profiling must be distribution-aware: the same geometric MIA protocol applied to a Zipfian-trained model and a uniform-trained model will have dramatically different calibration requirements, and a flat-distribution model may require adversarially constructed probes (e.g., deliberately injecting rare canary sequences during training, per Jagielski et al. 2022) to manufacture the contrast signal that organic long-tail examples provide naturally in skewed-distribution models.

The implication is stark: models trained on proprietary or synthetic datasets where the auditor cannot inject canaries occupy a fundamentally different auditability class, and the geometric MIA framework as developed so far provides essentially no traction — without manufactured contrast signal and without knowledge of the training distribution's tail structure, the auditor cannot calibrate the baseline intrinsic dimensionality against which memorization attractors are supposed to stand out. This is not merely a practical inconvenience but a formal limitation analogous to the cryptographic notion of a black-box oracle: Maini et al. (2023) showed that even loss-based MIA methods degrade catastrophically when the auditor lacks a reference model trained on the same distribution, and the geometric analog is if anything more severe because intrinsic dimensionality baselines are more distribution-sensitive than loss baselines. The synthetic data case is particularly sharp: a model trained entirely on outputs from another model (e.g., distillation on GPT-4 outputs, as in Alpaca or Vicuna) has a training distribution whose tail structure is determined by the teacher's generation diversity, which the auditor cannot characterize without either access to the teacher or an astronomical number of queries — the tail is effectively cryptographically hidden behind the teacher's sampling process. One partial escape is model-internal consistency probing without distribution knowledge: if the auditor has black-box generation access, they can apply the Pythia-style approach of measuring representation drift under paraphrase — a memorized sequence will show lower representational variance under surface-form perturbation than a generalized one, and this signal does not require knowing the training distribution, only the ability to generate multiple surface variants of a candidate and compare their hidden states. However, this paraphrase-invariance test has a fundamental ceiling: for synthetic or proprietary datasets where the auditor does not know what to probe for — i.e., cannot construct candidate memorized sequences — the test requires an exponentially large search over possible inputs, making it computationally infeasible without additional side-channel information about training data content. The honest conclusion for AI governance is that third-party auditing of proprietary LLMs for memorization is currently unsolved at the technical level, and policy frameworks that assume auditors can verify memorization claims (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure compliance, training data disclosure requirements) are making technical assumptions that the geometric and statistical MIA literature does not yet support.

The minimum query budget for a single candidate sequence under paraphrase-invariance testing is not a fixed number but a function of the effect size you are trying to detect, and concrete estimates from the closest relevant work suggest it is uncomfortably large: Shi et al. (2024) in the Min-K% Prob paper implicitly require hundreds of queries per candidate to stabilize their scoring statistics, and paraphrase-invariance testing is strictly harder because you must also generate diverse paraphrases that preserve semantic content while varying surface form — a generation step that itself consumes queries and introduces variance. A principled lower bound comes from treating the test as a hypothesis test with effect size δ (the difference in output distribution variance between memorized and generalized sequences): for δ ~ 0.1 (a realistic estimate given that memorized sequences show roughly 10–15% lower perplexity variance under paraphrase in the Carlini et al. extraction experiments), a two-sample test at 80% power and p=0.05 requires approximately 200–400 paraphrase pairs per candidate sequence, putting the minimum budget in the low hundreds of queries per candidate before accounting for paraphrase generation cost. Sequence length interacts brutally with this budget: longer sequences have more surface positions to vary but also more positions where the model's output distribution is determined by local context rather than global memorization, so the signal-to-noise ratio decreases with length even as the number of testable positions increases — empirically, Carlini et al. found that extractable memorization peaks at sequence lengths of 50–200 tokens and degrades at both extremes, suggesting the paraphrase test is most efficient in that window. Model size scaling cuts in the opposite direction from what intuition suggests: larger models memorize more per parameter (Carlini et al. 2023 showed memorization scales approximately as log(model size) holding data fixed), but their representations are also higher-dimensional, meaning the paraphrase-invariance signal is spread across more dimensions and requires either dimensionality reduction or more queries to detect with equivalent power. The practical upshot is that for a 70B-parameter model and a 100-token candidate sequence, a statistically defensible paraphrase-invariance test likely requires 500–1000 queries per candidate, making genome-scale auditing (testing thousands of candidate sequences) cost approximately 10^6 queries — feasible for a well-resourced auditor with API access but prohibitive under rate-limited or paid-API conditions, which is precisely the access model most proprietary systems enforce.
